From this slumber of the recluses, which is apt to creep, at times, upon the most pious and devout, it is the Office of violent and sudden disease to awake us; and if we could trace no further than this the advantages of occasional suffering, we should be warranted in concluding that it is good for man to be thus afflicted.


DEPENDENCE IN SICKNESS.


Violent diseases show us our dependence upon one another. Man, unaided by his fellow-man, is the most weak and helpless of animals. Placed beyond the reach of the kind, watchful and sympathetic aid of others, his first malady would be his last and the lord of this lower world would sink under the first blow which should strike his brittle tenement. Take the most proud and fiery spirit which ever animated muscular and gigantic frame, one who disdains to be obliged, and spurns alike the control and the assistance of others. Stretch him on the bed of sickness, languishing, faint, and motionless. Where now is that surly independence, that irritable haughtiness of soul? Nay, where now is that resistless strength of limb, that mighty bone, and lofty step! Has it come to this that child may lead so untractable spirit, that child may contend with that withered arm?


It is a common remark that death is universal leveler. The same is true, in its degree, of sickness. When we are reduced to such weakness that we cannot help ourselves, we find that many, whom we despised, can essentially help us. We find that the meanest of our species can lay us under obligation which we can never discharge. We find ourselves at the mercy of those on whom, if we have ever bestowed thought, we have been accustomed to look down with pity or contempt. But from a sick bed it is impossible to look down on any one. On the contrary, appeal to you who have ever suffered, whether you have not sometimes gazed with grateful admiration at the patient, condescending, united Offices of affectionate fidelity and tender watchfulness, which have at once ennobled in your esteem and endeared to your affections the humblest of your species.

But it is the tendency of sickness not only to reduce our extravagant self-estimation, by exhibiting our solitary helplessness, but, by leading our friends to perform for us innumerable and nameless offices of affection, it confirms and fastens forever those tender Ties which bind us to each other. Often, indeed, it adds new strength to the attachments of consanguinity, and new delicacy to the bonds of friendship. Often, in the chamber of the sick, stern temper has been melted to forgiveness, Indifference has ripened into love, aversion has changed into regard, and regard mellowed into attachment.


SICKNESS TEACHES US THE VALUE OF HEALTH


In the present state of refined and luxurious society, there are two large and increasing descriptions of men, to whom it is of no little importance to understand the real value of health. The first is the numerous class of imaginary invalids, who, though subject only to the unavoidable infirmities of mortality, create to themselves host of fancied ills and waste really healthful life in perpetual apprehensions, ungrateful complaints, idle imprecations, and uninterrupted discomfort. It is well known that such men never felt the severity of serious and painful illness. A single rude and violent attack of real disorder would soon shake off this cluster of uneasiness, and put to flight the cowardly tribe of imaginary woes. It would be good for these men to be afflicted indeed. There is, however, a precise opposite class composed of the presumptuous, thoughtless, and adventurous, nor adversely wise. Ignorant of the value of blessing which to youth is so common, they delight rashly to expose it, and insensibly to waste it away. After experience has counseled, friendship entreated, and authority commanded in vain, disease comes at last and closes the presumptuous game; and teaches them that health, strength, and life, though they may be possessed without gratitude, cannot be sported with without loss, or won back again by dexterity or courage.

It is the distinguishing mark of habitual piety to be grateful for the most common and ordinary blessings. There is no man so sensible and vile as not to feel glow of thankfulness for distinguishing favors or wonderful interpositions. But sickness discovers the value of the usual and customary degree of health and reminds the convalescent that he has scarcely thanked God for a blessing, in the place of which nothing can be substituted and for whose recovery everything but innocence may justly be surrendered.


FAMILY PRAYER.—In binding family together in peace and love, there is no human influence like that of domestic prayer. Uniting them in common object, it unites their sympathies and desires. Raising their hearts to heaven, it brings them altogether in the presence of God. The family altar is one to which they repair from the cares and toils of life. Reminding them of the rest reserved in heaven, it unites them in efforts of faith and obedience for its attainment. Earth has no holier spot than house thus sanctified by prayer; where the voice of supplication and thanksgiving consecrates every day; where the Word of God is devoutly read, and young and old unite to show forth His praise. It may be humble, but it is holy, and therefore heavenly.

Johnson received orders, as to the form and manner of charge, from Gen. Harrison in person, in the face and almost in sight of the enemy. "Rise up, my good fellow, my trusty companion."

John rose and Matty looked like three-tailed Bashaw.
Quoth Matty, "now bark, John mind—now—do you
You stumbled and alter'd and was beaten last year;
Do you see my long spurs the shanks only are GOLD,
The rowels STEEL John—mark well—you are told."
Old Tip wore no spurs; but held in his hand
The torn Constitution, and laws of the land,
Scarce enough of them left to be understood,
Yet he folded them up as well as he could;
And these were his saddle and 'twas thrown on rough,
With the girth of the Union 'twas buckled on tight.
With an unruffled brow, and hearty good will,
Looking cool as farmer just starting for mill.
Tip mounted his nag and thus addressed Bill:
No long exhortation shall now stop to make,
The cause is the people's, their interests the stake;
No matter to us if we're beat—none at all,
I've my log cabin left, and you've warm stall.

But the people expect the top notch of our speed,
And truly, friend Bill, of this there's great need.
I've no spur, nor whip, the twig I've just broke
From the wide spreading boughs of the old Charter;
None other you need save your own honest pride,
The people remember, be your speed and your guide.

Both riders, now ready, rein'd out of the crowd,
As they came alongside, each gracefully bowed.
"Good morning, my Tippy," quoth Mat. "this is kind,
Hope, by my soul, you'll not be far behind.
I would give me such pleasure to chat through the,
But John is devil, you know in his way.
He's so hard on the h and so cursedly fast,
That our contemplation fear won't last."
Old Tip nodded thanks, and said in reply,
"Crafty John ready and ready was Bill,
But sly Matty lingered his goblet to fill
His bright golden goblet (what democrat whim!) I'd
Tom Benton now brought him. Fill up to the brim.
Much oblig'd, but on cider try it again."

The starting bell struck—Old Tip loosed the rein,
And away Billy flew over hill and plain.
The way he clear'd Hartford, the county and all,
Was caution—just so he will do it next fall.
The Middlesex border Bill reach'd in short space,
The roads were there rougher, and he slackened his.
How strange the misfortune that happened to John,
He gallop'd it's true, but he could not get on.
He stepped fast enough, but 'twas straight up & down,
Like horse in the circus when rode by clown.

Some were sadly surprised, some said, never mind,
He'll soon take leap and leave Billy behind.
At length he cut dirt, like colt in a fright,
But 'twas sideways and railways and all ways but.
With much tribulation they hustled him through,
And Middlesex reached, he prick up anew.
"My goodness, this will do!
We're gaining—we're up—neck to neck, side to side,
Now go my Johnny, or I'll strip off your hide!"
On the way the few—but Johnny outsped,
He enter'd New-Haven—stop, faith I'd forgot.
His fore feet were there, but his hind legs not.

All Matty, ah Johnny what reverse in your fate,
Just now you were leading at wonderful rate!
What spell has come over you? Why that up and
As a ship fast aground, with her canvass all spread,
Rises up with the swell, but moves not ahead;
Or knave on the wheel, tho the wheel goes around,
Yet his own foolish self still holds the ground.
Old Tip now came up, and pass'd short way ahead,
But saw Matty's trouble, and turn'd him, and said,
"What's the matter, dear Matty, come spur up your—"
"Has Johnny the bots? till he's well shall wait—"
"Go to hell with your waiting, the state too if you
Choose, a few wooden nutmegs is not much to lose."

Honest Bill heard Matty's blessing & wheeling around,
Clear the counties remaining with at bound,
Thus cover'd with glory, and long before night.
Honest Bill and old Tip came in on the right,
There was joy and glad shouting with old and the young,
And honest Bill's praises and old Tip's were sung.

ing which I noticed in my first despatch to-day was
distinguished by speeches of great ability, which,
when published, will produce great effect in the
country. I mean the speeches of Mr. EVANS, of
